1.1Linear algebra essentials

  • Vector / matrix: data point x ∈ ℝd; dataset X ∈ ℝn×d; weights W ∈ ℝdout×din. A linear layer is a matrix multiply plus bias: y = Wx + b.
  • Norms: ‖x‖1=Σ|xi| (sparsity), ‖x‖2=√Σxi2 (energy), ‖x‖∞=max|xi|. Frobenius norm ‖A‖F=√ΣΣaij2.
  • Rank = number of independent columns. Low-rank structure underlies PCA, LoRA, matrix factorisation and attention approximations.
  • Eigen-decomposition: A v = λ v. For symmetric A: A = QΛQT with orthonormal Q. Covariance matrices are symmetric positive semi-definite (all λ ≥ 0).
  • SVD: any matrix A = UΣVT. Singular values σi measure importance of each direction; truncating to top-k gives the best rank-k approximation (Eckart–Young).
  • Positive definite matrix: xTAx > 0 ∀x≠0 → convex quadratic, unique minimum. The Hessian being PSD ⇔ local convexity.

  • Expectation is linear: E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y]. Variance: Var(X)=E[X²]−E[X]²; Var(X+Y)=Var X+Var Y+2Cov(X,Y).
  • Law of Large Numbers: sample mean → true mean. Central Limit Theorem: mean of n i.i.d. samples ≈ N(μ, σ²/n) — the reason confidence intervals and z-tests work.
  • Independence ⇒ uncorrelated, but not vice-versa (except for jointly Gaussian variables).
  • MLE: θ̂ = argmax Σ log p(xi|θ). MAP: adds log-prior. Gaussian prior ⇒ L2 regularisation; Laplace prior ⇒ L1 regularisation.

Entropy H(p) = −Σ p log p Cross-entropy H(p,q) = −Σ p log q KL(p‖q) = Σ p log(p/q) = H(p,q)

− H(p)

  • KL divergence ≥ 0, asymmetric. Minimising cross-entropy against fixed labels ≡ minimising KL ≡ maximising likelihood. Forward KL(p‖q) is mean-seeking; reverse KL(q‖p) is mode-seeking (used in VAEs/variational inference).
  • Mutual information I(X;Y)=KL(P(X,Y)‖P(X)P(Y)) — used in feature selection and representation learning (InfoNCE / contrastive loss).
  • Perplexity = exp(cross-entropy per token): the effective branching factor of a language model.

ConceptDefinitionInterview note
p-valueP(data at least this extreme | H₀ true)NOT the probability H₀ is true
Type I / II errorFalse positive (α) / false negative (β)Power = 1−β; increase n or effect size to raise power
Confidence intervalProcedure covering true value in 95% of repeatsNot ‘95% chance the value lies here’

COMMON TRAP Peeking at an A/B test daily and stopping when p < 0.05 inflates the false-positive rate. Use a fixed horizon, sequential testing (SPRT, alpha-spending) or Bayesian methods.

1.4Optimisation theory

  • Convex function: f(λx+(1−λ)y) ≤ λf(x)+(1−λ)f(y). Every local minimum is global. Linear/logistic regression and SVMs are convex; neural networks are non-convex but work in practice thanks to over-parameterisation, saddle-point escape and good initialisation.
  • Gradient descent: θ ← θ − η∇L(θ). For an L-smooth convex function, η ≤ 1/L guarantees convergence at rate O(1/k). Strongly convex → linear rate.
  • Newton’s method: θ ← θ − H−1∇L — quadratic convergence but O(d³) per step; quasi-Newton (L-BFGS) approximates H.
  • Lagrange / KKT: constrained optimisation min f(x) s.t. g(x)≤0 → L = f + λg; KKT conditions give SVM dual and its support vectors.
  • Stochastic gradients are unbiased estimates with variance ∝ 1/batch size; noise helps escape sharp minima (better generalisation).
ADVANCED Hessian eigenvalues explain training dynamics: a large ratio λm /λm (condition number) means narrow valleys and slow, oscillating SGD — the motivation for momentum, adaaxptivine optimisers and normalisation layers.

2.2Bias–variance trade-off & generalisation

E[(y − f̂(x))²] = Bias²[f̂(x)] + Var[f̂(x)] + σ²no

noise

SymptomDiagnosisFixes

ADVANCED Double descent: in modern over-parameterised networks test error can fall again after the interpolation threshold — classical U-shape is not the whole story. Implicit regularisation of SGD and large-scale data explain why huge models generalise.

2.3Linear & logistic models

  • Linear regression: ŷ = wTx + b. Closed form (normal equation) w = (XTX)−1XTy; equals MLE under Gaussian noise. Assumptions: linearity, independent errors, homoscedasticity, no multicollinearity (else XTX is near-singular → use Ridge).
  • Logistic regression: p(y=1|x)=σ(wTx+b), σ(z)=1/(1+e−z). Loss (log-loss / BCE): −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]. Gradient is elegantly XT(p − y)/n — same form as linear regression.
  • Softmax regression: pk=ezk/Σezj; gradient of CE w.r.t. logits = p − y (one-hot).
  • GLMs generalise: Gaussian→identity link, Bernoulli→logit, Poisson→log. Pick the family matching your target.

shrinks.

RegulariserPenaltyEffectBayesian view
L2 / Ridgeλ‖w‖₂²Shrinks all weights, handles collinearity, closed formGaussian prior
L1 / Lassoλ‖w‖₁Sparse solution → feature selectionLaplace prior
Elastic Netλ₁‖w‖₁ + λ₂‖w‖₂²Sparsity + stability for correlated featuresMixed
Dropout / weight decayImplicit / decoupledStandard in deep nets (AdamW decouples decay)Approx. model averaging

2.4Tree-based models & ensembles

  • Decision tree: greedy top-down splits maximising information gain (or Gini decrease). Handles mixed types and non-linearities, invariant to monotonic scaling, but high variance → prune, limit depth, or ensemble.
  • Random Forest = bagging + random feature subsets per split. Reduces variance; out-of-bag (OOB) error gives free validation; feature importance via impurity or permutation.
  • Gradient Boosting: fit each new tree to the negative gradient (pseudo-residual) of the loss: Fm(x)=Fm− (x)+η·hm(x). Reduces bias; needs shrinkage η, subsampling and early stopping to avoid overfitting. mm−1m
LibraryKey ideasBest for
XGBoost2nd-order Taylor of loss (gradient g and Hessian h); leaf weight w* = −G/(H+λ); regularised objective; sparsity-aware splitsStrong general baseline for tabular data
LightGBMHistogram binning, leaf-wise growth, GOSS sampling, EFB feature bundlingVery large datasets, speed
CatBoostOrdered boosting + ordered target statistics to avoid target leakage; symmetric treesMany high-cardinality categoricals
INTERVIEW TIP For tabular data, well-tuned gradient-boosted trees usually beat deep learning. Say this confidently, then explain the exceptions: very large data, multimodal inputs, or when embeddings must be learned end-to-end.

2.5SVM, kNN, Naive Bayes

  • SVM: min ½‖w‖² + C Σ max(0, 1 − yi(wTxi+b)) (hinge loss). Kernel trick: replace xTx′ with k(x,x′) (RBF: exp(−γ‖x−x′‖²)) to get non-linear boundaries without explicit features. Large C → less regularisation. Scales poorly (O(n²–n³)).
  • k-NN: non-parametric, lazy; prediction = majority/mean of k nearest neighbours. Needs feature scaling; suffers from the curse of dimensionality (distances concentrate). Use ANN indices (HNSW, FAISS) at scale.
  • Naive Bayes: P(y|x) ∝ P(y)ΠP(xi|y) assuming conditional independence. Surprisingly strong for text; fast; probabilities are poorly calibrated.

2.6Unsupervised learning

  • k-means: alternate assign → update centroids to minimise within-cluster SS. Sensitive to init (use k-means++), assumes spherical clusters, choose k via elbow / silhouette / gap statistic.
  • GMM + EM: soft clustering; E-step computes responsibilities, M-step re-estimates μ, Σ, π. Generalises k-means (covariance = σ²I, σ→0).
  • DBSCAN: density-based, finds arbitrary shapes and noise; parameters ε and minPts. Hierarchical: agglomerative with linkage (Ward, average).
  • PCA: centre data, eigen-decompose covariance (or SVD of X); project on top-k components; explained variance ratio = λk/Σλ. Linear. t-SNE / UMAP: non-linear, for visualisation — distances between clusters are not meaningful.
  • Anomaly detection: Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, autoencoder reconstruction error, Mahalanobis distance.

2.7Recommender systems

ApproachIdeaPros / cons
Content-basedMatch item features to user profileNo cold-start for items; limited serendipity
Collaborative filteringUsers with similar history like similar itemsPowerful; cold-start & sparsity problems
Matrix factorisationR ≈ UVT minimising Σ(r−u·v)² + λ(‖U‖²+‖V‖²) (ALS/SGD)Scalable; implicit feedback via weighted MF
Two-tower retrievalUser and item encoders; dot-product; ANN searchMillisecond retrieval over millions of items

KEY IDEA Industrial recommenders are multi-stage: candidate generation (recall, ~10³ from 10⁷) → ranking (precision) → re-ranking (diversity, business rules). Discuss exploration (bandits) and position bias.

COMMON TRAP ROC-AUC can look great on a 1:1000 imbalanced problem while precision is terrible. Report PR-AUC and precision@k for rare-event tasks, and pick the threshold from business cost, not 0.5.

3.3Validation strategy & data leakage

  • Hold-out (train/val/test) for large data; k-fold CV for small data; stratified k-fold keeps class ratios; group k-fold when samples of one entity (user, patient) must not straddle splits; time-series split (expanding window) for temporal data — never shuffle.
  • Nested CV: inner loop tunes hyper-parameters, outer loop estimates generalisation — avoids optimistic bias.
  • Leakage = information at training that will not exist at prediction time: target-derived features, future data, fitting scalers/encoders on the full dataset, duplicates across splits, post-event features. Always fit preprocessing inside the training fold (use sklearn Pipeline).
INTERVIEW TIP When a model shows suspiciously good validation metrics, your first hypothesis should be leakage, not brilliance. Inspect top feature importances for anything that ‘knows the future’.

3.4Imbalanced data

TechniqueHow it worksCaveat
Class weights / cost-sensitive lossMultiply loss of minority classSimple first choice; keep probabilities recalibrated
ResamplingOver-sample minority (SMOTE interpolates neighbours) / under-sample majorityResample only the training fold; SMOTE can create noisy samples
Focal loss−α(1−pt)γ log pt; down-weights easy examplesPopular in detection (RetinaNet)
Threshold movingChoose operating point on PR curveFree; do it before anything fancy

3.5Feature engineering & preprocessing

TopicPractices
ScalingStandardise (z-score) for linear/SVM/NN/kNN; min-max for bounded inputs; trees do not need it. Log-transform heavy tails.
Categorical encodingOne-hot (low cardinality), ordinal (ordered), target/mean encoding with K-fold + smoothing (avoid leakage), hashing trick, learned embeddings (high cardinality).
Missing valuesImpute median/mode/model-based; add ‘is_missing’ indicator; understand MCAR / MAR / MNAR; trees like XGBoost handle NaN natively.
OutliersWinsorise/clip, robust scalers, or use robust losses (Huber); never blindly delete signal.
Text / time / geoTF-IDF, embeddings; cyclical encoding sin/cos of hour/day; lag & rolling-window features; geohash / distance features.
Feature selectionFilter (mutual information, variance), wrapper (RFE), embedded (L1, tree importance), permutation importance, SHAP.
DimensionalityPCA / autoencoders; remove highly correlated features (VIF > 10 indicates multicollinearity).

3.6Interpretability & calibration

  • SHAP: Shapley-value attributions — additive, consistent; TreeSHAP is exact and fast for trees. LIME: local linear surrogate. PDP / ICE plots show marginal effects; permutation importance measures drop in score.
  • Calibration: predicted 0.8 should be right 80% of the time. Fix with Platt scaling (sigmoid), isotonic regression, or temperature scaling for neural nets; visualise with reliability diagrams.

4.1Neural networks & backpropagation

(l)(l)(l−1)(l)(L) h(l) = σ( W(l) h(l− + b(l) ) , ŷ = h(L) , θ ← θ − η ∇θ L(ŷ, y)

  • Universal approximation: a wide enough single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact set — but depth gives exponentially more efficient representations.
  • Backprop = reverse-mode automatic differentiation: one forward pass caches activations, one backward pass computes all gradients at cost ≈ 2–3× the forward pass. Memory is dominated by stored activations (→ gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory).
  • Autograd frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) build a dynamic graph; loss.backward() accumulates gradients — remember optimizer.zero_grad().
  • Shape discipline: for a batch X (B×din) and layer W (din×dou ), dL/dW = XT·(dL/dY), dL/dX = (dL/dY)·WT. ininout

4.4Initialisation & gradient problems

InitVarianceFor
Xavier / Glorot2/(nin+nout)tanh / sigmoid
He / Kaiming2/ninReLU family
Small normal (0.02)fixedTransformers (GPT-2 style), with residual-scaled output layers
  • Vanishing gradients: product of many derivatives < 1. Remedies: ReLU/GELU, proper init, residual connections, normalisation, LSTM/GRU gating.
  • Exploding gradients: product > 1 (RNNs especially). Remedies: gradient clipping (clip global norm to 1.0), smaller LR, careful init.
  • Dead ReLUs / loss spikes: lower LR, warm-up, check data (NaNs, bad labels), use bf16 rather than fp16, add z-loss.

INTERVIEW TIP Learning rate is the single most important hyper-parameter. Use an LR range test, warm-up for the first 0.5–2% of steps, and scale LR roughly ∝ √(batch size) (or linearly with warm-up) when you change batch size.

4.6Regularisation & normalisation

TechniqueWhat it doesNotes

LayerNorm / RMSNormNormalise across features per tokenStandard in Transformers; RMSNorm drops mean-centering (faster)

Label smoothingSoft targets (1−ε, ε/(K−1))Prevents over-confidence

4.7Practical training checklist

  • Overfit a tiny batch first (loss → ~0) to prove the model and pipeline can learn.
  • Sanity-check the initial loss: for K classes it should be ≈ ln K.
  • Log train/val loss, gradient norm, LR, activation statistics, throughput; watch for NaNs.
  • Mixed precision (bf16 preferred over fp16 — no loss scaling), gradient accumulation for large effective batch, EMA of weights, seed everything, checkpoint often.
  • Change one thing at a time; keep an experiment tracker (Weights & Biases, MLflow).

5.1Convolution mechanics

Output size O = ⌊(N + 2P − K) / S⌋ + 1 Params (conv) = (K·K·Cin + 1) · Cou

inout

  • Inductive biases: locality, weight sharing, translation equivariance — far fewer parameters than a fully-connected layer on pixels.
  • Receptive field grows with depth, stride and dilation. Pooling gives small translation invariance; global average pooling replaces big FC heads.
  • 1×1 convolution mixes channels cheaply (bottlenecks); depthwise-separable conv (MobileNet) cuts cost ≈ 8–9×; dilated conv enlarges receptive field without pooling; transposed conv upsamples.
  • Worked example: 3×3 conv, 64→128 channels has (9·64+1)·128 = 73,856 parameters.

5.2Landmark architectures

ModelYearKey ideaImpact
LeNet / AlexNet1998 / 2012ReLU, dropout, GPU trainingStarted deep-learning era
VGG2014Stacks of 3×3 convsSimplicity; heavy FC layers

TaskModelsConcepts

5.3.1 Transfer learning recipe

  • Small data: freeze backbone, train new head → unfreeze top blocks with 10× smaller LR (discriminative LRs).
  • Match preprocessing (mean/std, resolution) to pretraining. Fine-tune with strong augmentation; monitor for catastrophic forgetting.
  • Deployment: quantisation (INT8), pruning, distillation, ONNX/TensorRT, channels-last layout.
INTERVIEW TIP Be ready to explain why ResNet works: the identity shortcut lets gradients flow unimpeded (∂y/∂x = ∂F/∂x + 1), and the block only has to learn a residual — easier to optimise than a full mapping.

06 · Sequence Models: RNN, LSTM, GRU

🎯 IN THIS CHAPTER · 1 SECTIONS

  • Sequence Models: RNN, LSTM, GRU

6Sequence Models: RNN, LSTM, GRU

  • RNN: ht = tanh(Whht− + Wxxt + b). Shares weights across time; processes variable-length input but is sequential (no parallel1ism) and forgets long-range context.
  • Backprop Through Time (BPTT): unroll the network; gradient contains Π ∂ht/∂ht− → vanishes (‖W‖<1) or tt−1 explodes (‖W‖>1). Truncated BPTT + gradient clipping is standard.
GateRoleEquation
Forget ftWhat to erase from memoryσ(Wf[ht−1,xt]+bf)
Input itWhat new info to writeσ(Wi[ht−1,xt]+bi)
Output otWhat to expose as htσ(Wo[ht−1,xt]+bo)
Cell updateAdditive path → stable gradientsCt = ft⊙Ct−1 + it⊙tanh(Wc[·]+bc)
  • GRU: merges cell and hidden state, two gates (update z, reset r) → ~25% fewer parameters, similar accuracy.
  • Bidirectional RNN reads both directions (for tagging, not for generation). Seq2Seq: encoder compresses input to a vector, decoder generates output; the fixed-size bottleneck motivated attention (Bahdanau, 2014) which lets the decoder look back at all encoder states — the seed of the Transformer.
  • Why Transformers replaced RNNs: parallel training over the sequence, O(1) path length between any two tokens, better scaling. RNN-like models return in linear-time forms: state-space models (S4, Mamba) and RWKV, offering O(n) inference with constant memory.
AspectRNN/LSTMTransformerSSM (Mamba)
Training parallelismSequentialFully parallelParallel scan
Long-range dependencyWeakStrong (global attention)Strong, compressed state
Compute per token (inference)O(1)O(n) with KV-cacheO(1)
Memory over contextO(1)O(n)O(1)

07 · Transformers — Deep Dive

🎯 IN THIS CHAPTER · 3 SECTIONS

  • Architecture components & modern upgrades
  • Parameter & compute accounting
  • Tokenisation

Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax( Q KT / √dk + M ) V MultiHead = Concat(head1…headh) WO

  • Intuition: each token issues a query; every token offers a key (what I contain) and a value (what I give). Similarity(query,key) → softmax weights → weighted sum of values.
  • Why divide by √dk: dot products of dk-dim random vectors have variance dk; without scaling, softmax saturates and gradients vanish.
  • Multi-head: h parallel subspaces (dk = d/h) let different heads specialise (syntax, coreference, position…). Cost is the same as one big head.
  • Causal mask M (−∞ above the diagonal) stops a token seeing the future — required for autoregressive language models.
  • Complexity: time O(n²·d), memory O(n²) for the score matrix — the bottleneck for long contexts. Feed-forward layers cost O(n·d²).

7.1Architecture components & modern upgrades

ComponentOriginal (2017)Modern LLM practiceWhy
Positional infoSinusoidal absoluteRoPE (rotate q,k by position angle); ALiBiRelative position, better length extrapolation
NormalisationPost-LN LayerNormPre-LN + RMSNormStable training of deep stacks; cheaper
FFN activationReLU, hidden 4dSwiGLU, hidden ≈ 8d/3Higher quality per FLOP
Attention headsMulti-Head (MHA)GQA / MQA: share K,V across head groupsShrinks KV-cache 4–8×, faster decoding
Attention kernelNaive n×nFlashAttention (tiling in SRAM, exact)O(n) memory, 2–4× faster, IO-aware
Bias termsYesRemovedSimplicity, stability
SparsityDenseMixture-of-Experts (top-k routing)More parameters at constant FLOPs
Context512–2k128k–1M+ (RoPE scaling, YaRN, ring attention)Long documents, agents

7.2Parameter & compute accounting

Params per layer ≈ 12 d² (4d² attention + 8d² FFN) Total ≈ 12·L·d² + V·d

  • GPT-3: L=96, d=12,288 → 12·96·12288² ≈ 174B (+ embeddings) ≈ 175B.
  • Training FLOPs ≈ 6·N·D (N params, D tokens); inference ≈ 2·N FLOPs per token.
  • KV-cache per token = 2 · L · nk · dh · bytes. LLaMA-2-70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads, dhe =128, fp16) ≈ kv_headsheadhead 320 KB/token → 4k context ≈ 1.3v_GheBadpser seeqaudence.
  • Mixture-of-Experts: total parameters ≫ active parameters (Mixtral-8×7B ≈ 47B total, ≈ 13B active). Needs a load-balancing loss and expert-parallel communication.

7.3Tokenisation

  • BPE / byte-level BPE merges frequent byte pairs; WordPiece (BERT) maximises likelihood; SentencePiece / Unigram is language-agnostic. Vocabulary sizes 32k–256k.
  • Trade-off: larger vocab → shorter sequences but bigger embedding/softmax and rarer tokens. Tokenisation explains odd behaviour on arithmetic, spelling, rare languages and code whitespace.
  • Embedding matrix is often tied with the output projection to save parameters.
FamilyObjectiveExamplesBest at
Encoder-onlyMasked LM (predict masked tokens)BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTaClassification, retrieval embeddings, NER
Decoder-onlyNext-token prediction (causal)GPT, LLaMA, Claude, MistralOpen-ended generation, in-context learning
Encoder-decoderSpan corruption / seq2seqT5, BART, WhisperTranslation, summarisation, speech
INTERVIEW TIP Classic question: ‘Why does a Transformer need positional encoding?’ — Self-attention is permutation-equivariant; without position signals the model sees a bag of tokens.

8.1Pre-training & scaling laws

  • Data: web crawl (deduplicated, quality-filtered), code, books, papers, multilingual, synthetic data. Deduplication, decontamination against benchmarks and PII removal matter as much as quantity.
  • Objective: maximise Σ log p(xt | x< ) over trillions of tokens. Emergent abilities (in-context learning, reasoning) appear with scale and data quality.t
  • Scaling laws (Kaplan, Chinchilla): L(N,D) = E + A/Nα + B/Dβ. Compute-optimal ≈ 20 tokens per parameter; but production models are deliberately over-trained (LLaMA-3-8B saw ~15T tokens) because inference cost dominates over the model’s lifetime.

Compute C ≈ 6 N D FLOPs Optimal: N ∝ C0.5 , D ∝ C0.5

8.2Adaptation: prompting, fine-tuning, PEFT

MethodWhat changesWhen to useCost
Prompting / few-shot / CoTNothing (context only)First attempt always≈ free
RAGAdds retrieved knowledge to contextFresh / private knowledge, citationsLow
Full fine-tuning (SFT)All weightsLarge data, deep behaviour changeVery high
LoRALow-rank adapters ΔW = BADomain/style adaptation on modest hardwareLow
QLoRALoRA on 4-bit NF4 quantised baseFine-tune 30–70B on a single GPUVery low
Adapters / Prefix / Prompt tuningSmall inserted modules or soft promptsMulti-task servingLow
DistillationSmall student mimics large teacherLatency / cost reductionMedium
  • LoRA hyper-parameters: rank r (8–64), α (often 2r), target modules (q,k,v,o and MLP), dropout. Adapters can be merged into W₀ for zero inference overhead or hot-swapped per tenant.
  • Rule of thumb: fine-tune to teach format, style, behaviour and skills; use RAG to supply facts. Fine-tuning on new facts is unreliable and can increase hallucination.
  • Common SFT pitfalls: low-quality or inconsistent data, format mismatch with chat template, catastrophic forgetting (mix in general data, lower LR), evaluating on training prompts.

8.3Alignment: RLHF, DPO, GRPO

MethodIdeaKey equation / note
RLHF (PPO)Train a reward model on human preference pairs; optimise policy with PPO + KL penalty to reference modelmax E[r(x,y)] − β·KL(π‖πref). Needs 4 models in memory; unstable
DPODirectly optimise preferences without RL or explicit reward modelL = −log σ( β[ log π(yw|x)/πref(yw|x) − log π(yl|x)/πref(yl|x) ] )
GRPO / RLVRSample a group of answers, advantage = (ri − mean)/std within the group; verifiable rewards (unit tests, math answers); no value networkPowers recent reasoning models; reward hacking is the risk
Constitutional AI / RLAIFAI feedback guided by written principles replaces some human labelsScalable oversight
Best-of-N / rejection samplingSample N, keep highest-reward output for SFT or servingSimple, strong baseline
ADVANCED PPO clipped objective: L = E[ min( rt(θ)At , clip(rt(θ), 1−ε, 1+ε) At ) ], where rt = πθ(a|s)/πold(a|s). The clip keeps each update inside a trust region without second-order machinery.

8.4Decoding & sampling

StrategyMechanismEffect
Greedyargmax each stepDeterministic, repetitive
Beam searchKeep top-B partial sequencesGood for translation; bland for chat
Temperature Tsoftmax(z/T)T<1 sharper, T>1 more random
Top-kSample from k most likely tokensCuts long tail
Top-p (nucleus)Smallest set with cumulative prob ≥ pAdaptive cut-off; p≈0.9
Min-p, typical, repetition/frequency penaltiesRefined truncation and anti-repetitionQuality tuning

8.5Efficient inference

  • Prefill vs decode: prefill processes the prompt in parallel (compute-bound); decode generates one token at a time (memory-bandwidth bound — every step re-reads all weights + KV-cache).
  • KV-cache stores past keys/values so each new token costs O(n) instead of recomputing O(n²). Managed with PagedAttention (vLLM) to avoid fragmentation; continuous batching inserts new requests every step; prefix caching reuses shared prompts.
  • Quantisation: FP16/BF16 → FP8 / INT8 / INT4 (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF) — 2–4× smaller and faster with small quality loss; KV-cache quantisation for long contexts.
  • Speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes k tokens, the large model verifies them in one pass — same output distribution, 2–3× speed-up. Also Medusa/EAGLE heads.
  • Others: FlashAttention, tensor-parallel serving, model distillation, sliding-window attention, MoE routing, request scheduling and autoscaling.
MetricMeaningTypical target
TTFTTime to first token (prefill latency)< 500 ms for chat
TPOT / ITLTime per output token20–50 ms (≈ 20–50 tok/s per user)
MetricMeaningTypical target

Throughput Tokens/s across all requests Maximise per GPU-$

Cost $ per 1M input / output tokens Output tokens cost 3–5× input

8.6Evaluation, hallucination, safety

  • Benchmarks: MMLU/MMLU-Pro (knowledge), GSM8K/MATH (reasoning), HumanEval/SWE-bench (code), IFEval (instruction following), MT-Bench / Arena Elo (chat preference), long-context needle tests. Beware contamination and saturation; always build a task-specific eval set.
  • LLM-as-judge: cheap and scalable but biased (position, verbosity, self-preference). Use pairwise comparisons, swap order, calibrate against human labels.
  • Hallucination mitigation: retrieval grounding + citations, lower temperature, ask for uncertainty, self-consistency / verification steps, tool use, constrained output, abstain option, fine-tune on refusals.
  • Safety: prompt injection (direct & indirect), jailbreaks, data exfiltration, PII leakage. Defences: input/output classifiers, privilege separation, tool allow-lists, sandboxing, human approval for risky actions, red-teaming.

8.7Prompt engineering patterns

PatternDescription
Few-shotProvide 2–8 input→output examples matching format and edge cases
Chain-of-ThoughtAsk the model to reason step-by-step before answering; boosts maths & logic
Self-consistencySample several reasoning paths, majority-vote the answer
ReActInterleave Thought → Action (tool call) → Observation
Role / system promptFix persona, rules, format; put stable instructions first (enables prefix caching)
Structured outputJSON schema / function-calling; validate and retry on parse failure
Decomposition / prompt chainingSplit a complex task into verified stages

Reciprocal Rank Fusion: RRF(d) = Σr∈ 1 / (k + rankr(d)) , k ≈ 60

r∈ rankersr

ANN indexIdeaTrade-off
Flat (brute force)Exact scan100% recall, O(N) — fine up to ~10⁵–10⁶ vectors
IVFk-means partitions; search nprobe nearest cellsFast; recall depends on nprobe
PQ / OPQCompress vectors to short codes10–50× less memory, lossy

  • Bi-encoder (embed separately, fast, used for retrieval) vs cross-encoder (joint attention, accurate, slow, used for reranking).
  • Advanced RAG: query rewriting / multi-query, HyDE (embed a hypothetical answer), query decomposition for multi-hop, contextual chunk headers, GraphRAG (entity graph), self-RAG / corrective RAG, agentic RAG that decides when and what to retrieve.
  • Failure analysis: separate retrieval failures (right chunk not in top-k) from generation failures (chunk present, answer wrong). Watch for ‘lost in the middle’ — put the most relevant chunks first/last.
  • Production: cache embeddings and answers, stream tokens, per-tenant access control, incremental re-indexing, freshness policies, observability (trace every retrieval), cost/latency budgets.
INTERVIEW TIP When asked ‘RAG vs fine-tuning?’ answer: RAG for knowledge (updatable, attributable, secure), fine-tuning for behaviour/format, and often both. Then add how you would measure each.

9.2AI agents

  • Agent = LLM + tools + memory + control loop. Tools are described by JSON schemas (function calling); open standards like Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardise tool/data connections.
  • Patterns: ReAct; plan-and-execute; reflection / self-critique; router (pick a specialist); orchestrator-workers; multi-agent debate; human-in-the-loop approval for irreversible actions.
  • Memory: short-term (context window), long-term (vector store / database), episodic summaries; manage context growth with summarisation and retrieval.
  • Reliability: constrain tool permissions, validate arguments, idempotent tools, timeouts and retries, step limits to prevent loops, deterministic workflows wherever a fixed pipeline suffices.
  • Evaluation: task success rate, trajectory/tool-call correctness, cost, latency, safety incidents; build regression suites of scripted scenarios and trace every run.
KEY IDEA Prefer the simplest architecture that works: single prompt → prompt chain → workflow with tools → autonomous agent. Every extra degree of autonomy multiplies failure modes and cost.

10.1Diffusion in detail

Forward: xt = √ᾱt · x0 + √(1−ᾱt) · ε , ε~N(0,I) Loss: E ‖ε − εθ(xt, t, c)‖²

  • Latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion): a VAE compresses images (×8 per side) and diffusion runs in latent space — ~50× cheaper. Denoiser is a U-Net or Diffusion Transformer (DiT); text conditioning through cross-attention with CLIP/T5 embeddings.
  • Classifier-free guidance: ε̃ = εun + w·(εcon − εun ); larger w → stronger prompt adherence, lower uncondconduncond diversity.
  • Flow matching / rectified flow learn straight-line velocity fields → fewer steps; used by recent image/video models.
  • Control & personalisation: ControlNet (spatial conditions), LoRA / DreamBooth (subject/style), inpainting, image-to-image.
COMMON TRAP GAN discriminator loss going to zero is a bad sign — G is not learning. Monitor sample quality (FID), not just the losses.

11Reinforcement Learning

  • MDP = (S, A, P, R, γ). Policy π(a|s); value Vπ(s)=E[Σγtrt]; action-value Qπ(s,a); advantage A=Q−V.
  • Exploration vs exploitation: ε-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling, entropy bonuses. Multi-armed bandit = RL without state — used in ads, recommendations and A/B allocation.
FamilyAlgorithmsKey points
Value-basedQ-learning: Q(s,a) ← Q + α[r + γ maxaQ(s′,a′) − Q]; SARSA; DQN (replay buffer + target network)′Off-policy; discrete actions; overestimation → Double DQN
Policy gradientREINFORCE: ∇J = E[∇log π(a|s)·Gt]High variance → subtract baseline
Actor-criticA2C/A3C, PPO, TRPO, DDPG, TD3, SACCritic estimates V/Q to reduce variance; PPO clip = stable default; SAC for continuous control
Model-basedDyna, MuZero, DreamerLearn dynamics to plan → sample-efficient
Offline / imitationBehaviour cloning, CQL, DAgger, inverse RLLearn from logged data without exploration

Bellman optimality: Q*(s,a) = E[ r + γ · maxa′ Q*(s′,a′) ]

  • On-policy (PPO) needs fresh data but is stable; off-policy (DQN, SAC) reuses replay data and is sample-efficient.
  • Credit assignment, sparse rewards, reward hacking and sim-to-real gaps are the practical challenges; use reward shaping carefully.
  • Link to LLMs: RLHF treats generation as a bandit/MDP where the reward model scores the completion; GRPO/RLVR use verifiable rewards to train reasoning.

12.3Monitoring & drift

  • Data drift (P(X) changes), concept drift (P(y|X) changes), label / prior shift (P(y) changes), upstream data bugs (schema, units, nulls).
  • Detect with PSI = Σ(ai−ei)·ln(ai/ei) (<0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate, >0.25 major), KS test, JS-divergence, embedding drift; track prediction distribution and delayed-label performance.
  • Retraining triggers: schedule, drift threshold, performance drop, new data volume. Always keep a rollback model and a champion/challenger comparison.
  • Testing ML: data tests, unit tests for feature code, invariance and directional tests, slice-based evaluation (per segment fairness), load tests, and shadow comparisons.

13 · Distributed Training & Performance Engineering

StrategyWhat is splitCommunicationUse when
Data parallel (DDP)Batch; full model copy per GPUAll-reduce gradients each stepModel fits on one GPU
ZeRO-1/2 / FSDPOptimiser states → gradients → parameters shardedAll-gather params, reduce-scatter gradsModel too big for one GPU but layers fit

13.1Memory budgeting

Mixed-precision Adam: 2 (bf16 weights) + 2 (grads) + 4 (fp32 master) + 4 (m) + 4 (v) = 16 bytes /

parameter

  • A 7B model needs ≈ 7×16 = 112 GB for states alone (before activations) → shard with ZeRO-3/FSDP or use LoRA/QLoRA. Inference in fp16 ≈ 2 bytes/param = 14 GB; INT4 ≈ 3.5 GB.
  • Activation memory scales with batch × sequence × layers; reduce via gradient checkpointing (recompute, ≈ +30% compute), FlashAttention, smaller micro-batches + gradient accumulation.
  • Mixed precision: bf16 (same range as fp32, no loss-scaling) is preferred; fp16 needs dynamic loss scaling; FP8 on H100-class GPUs for higher throughput.

13.2Performance checklist

  • Roofline thinking: compute-bound (large matmuls) vs memory-bound (element-wise ops, decoding). Fuse kernels (torch.compile, Triton), use channels-last, pinned memory and async data loading.
  • Utilisation metric: MFU = achieved FLOPs / peak FLOPs; 40–55% is excellent for LLM training.
  • Data pipeline is often the bottleneck: parallel workers, prefetch, sharded formats (WebDataset, Parquet, Arrow), caching, avoid tiny files.
  • Debugging scale: check loss spikes, straggler GPUs, NCCL timeouts, non-determinism, checkpoint/resume correctness, and learning-rate/batch-size scaling.
  • Compression for deployment: quantisation (PTQ vs QAT), pruning (structured), distillation, low-rank factorisation, export via ONNX/TensorRT, dynamic batching.
INTERVIEW TIP Interviewers love back-of-envelope estimates: ‘How many GPUs to train a 70B model on 2T tokens in 30 days?’ → FLOPs = 6·70e9·2e12 = 8.4e23; at ~400 TFLOP/s peak × 40% MFU ≈ 1.6e14 FLOP/s per GPU → 5.2e9 GPU-s ≈ 1.46M GPU-hours → over 720 h ≈ ~2,000 GPUs.

14.1Multi-head causal self-attention (PyTorch)

import math, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, dropout=0.0):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        self.h, self.dk = n_heads, d_model // n_heads
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model, bias=False)
        self.out = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)
    def forward(self, x): # x: (B, T, C)
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        q, k, v = [t.view(B, T, self.h, self.dk).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v)] # (B,h,T,dk)
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.dk) # (B,h,T,T)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device, dtype=torch.bool), 1)
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf")).softmax(dim=-1)
        y = self.drop(att) @ v # (B,h,T,dk)
        return self.out(y.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, C))
# Production: use F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True) -> FlashAttention kernel

14.2Standard PyTorch training loop (AMP, clipping, scheduler)

model.train() # bf16 autocast -> no GradScaler required
for step, (x, y) in enumerate(loader):
    x, y = x.to(dev, non_blocking=True), y.to(dev, non_blocking=True)
    with torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        loss = criterion(model(x), y) / accum_steps
    loss.backward()
    if (step + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        optimizer.step(); scheduler.step(); optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    if step % 100 == 0: print(step, loss.item() * accum_steps)
@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate(model, loader):
    model.eval(); tot = n = 0
    for x, y in loader:
        p = model(x.to(dev)).argmax(-1).cpu(); tot += (p == y).sum().item(); n += len(y)
    return tot / n

14.3Logistic regression & k-means from scratch (NumPy)

import numpy as np
def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -50, 50)))
def fit_logreg(X, y, lr=0.1, epochs=500, l2=1e-3):
    n, d = X.shape; w, b = np.zeros(d), 0.0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        p = sigmoid(X @ w + b)
        w -= lr * (X.T @ (p - y) / n + l2 * w) # gradient of BCE + L2
        b -= lr * np.mean(p - y)
    return w, b
def kmeans(X, k, iters=100, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    C = X[rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)]
    for _ in range(iters):
        lab = np.argmin(((X[:, None, :] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1) # assign
        newC = np.array([X[lab == j].mean(0) if np.any(lab == j) else C[j] for j in range(k)])
        if np.allclose(newC, C): break
        C = newC
    return C, lab

14.4LoRA layer & ranking metrics

class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base: nn.Linear, r=8, alpha=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base
        for p in self.base.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False # freeze W0
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(r, base.in_features) * 0.01)
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(base.out_features, r)) # zero-init -> starts as base
        self.scale = alpha / r
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.base(x) + (x @ self.A.T @ self.B.T) * self.scale
def ndcg_at_k(rels, k): # rels: graded relevance in ranked order
    rels = np.asarray(rels, float)[:k]
    dcg = ((2 ** rels - 1) / np.log2(np.arange(2, len(rels) + 2))).sum()
    ideal = np.sort(rels)[::-1]
    idcg = ((2 ** ideal - 1) / np.log2(np.arange(2, len(ideal) + 2))).sum()
    return dcg / idcg if idcg > 0 else 0.0
def rrf(rankings, k=60): # rankings: list of ranked doc-id lists
    score = {}
    for r in rankings:
        for pos, d in enumerate(r, 1): score[d] = score.get(d, 0) + 1 / (k + pos)
    return sorted(score, key=score.get, reverse=True)

15 · Interview Q&A Bank

🎯 IN THIS CHAPTER · 31 QUESTIONS

  • Explain bias vs variance and how you would diagnose each.
  • Why does L1 give sparsity but L2 does not?
  • Precision vs recall — how do you choose a threshold?
  • Random forest vs gradient boosting?
  • …and more

15.1 Machine-learning fundamentals

Q1Explain bias vs variance and how you would diagnose each.

Bias = error from wrong/simple assumptions (underfit); variance = sensitivity to training sample (overfit). Compare train vs validation error and use learning curves: high both → bias; big gap → variance. Fix bias with capacity/features; fix variance with data, regularisation, ensembling.

Q2Why does L1 give sparsity but L2 does not?

The L1 constraint region has corners on the axes, so the optimum often lands where coordinates are exactly zero; the L2 ball is smooth, so it only shrinks. Equivalently the L1 subgradient is a constant push toward zero while L2’s shrinks proportionally to the weight.

Q3Precision vs recall — how do you choose a threshold?

Plot the PR curve, attach costs to FP and FN, and choose the operating point minimising expected cost or satisfying a constraint (e.g. recall ≥ 95%). Never default to 0.5, and recalibrate if probabilities are used downstream.

Q4Random forest vs gradient boosting?

RF: parallel deep trees, averaging reduces variance, robust with little tuning. GBM: shallow trees fitted sequentially to gradients, reduces bias, usually higher accuracy but needs tuning (η, depth, subsampling) and can overfit noisy labels.

Q5How do you handle missing data and categorical variables with high cardinality?

Impute with indicators (or use native NaN handling in trees); for high-cardinality categoricals use target encoding with out-of-fold statistics and smoothing, hashing, or learned embeddings; guard against leakage.

Q6What is data leakage? Give three examples.

Using information unavailable at prediction time: features derived from the target, fitting normalisation on the full dataset, and random splitting of time-series/grouped data. Detect through suspiciously high metrics and feature-importance audits.

Q7Explain PCA and when it fails.

PCA projects onto orthogonal directions of maximal variance (top eigenvectors of covariance / SVD). It is linear, scale-sensitive and variance ≠ relevance — a low-variance direction may be the discriminative one; use supervised methods (LDA) or non-linear embeddings.

Q8Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?

A trivial majority-class predictor scores 99% when positives are 1%. Use PR-AUC, recall/precision at a threshold, F-scores, MCC and cost-based metrics.

Q9How does k-fold cross-validation work and when not to use it?

Split into k folds, train on k−1, validate on the remaining, average. Avoid for time series (use forward chaining), grouped data (use group k-fold) or very expensive models (use a hold-out).

15.2 Deep learning

Q10Why is ReLU preferred over sigmoid?

Non-saturating for positive inputs (gradient 1), cheap, sparse activations; sigmoid saturates causing vanishing gradients and is not zero-centred.

Q11Explain BatchNorm — and why LayerNorm in Transformers?

BN normalises per channel across the batch, smoothing the loss landscape, allowing higher LR. It depends on batch statistics (bad for small batches/variable lengths, train≠eval). LN normalises each token across features — batch-independent and suited to sequences.

Q12What does Adam do and why AdamW?

Adam keeps exponential moving averages of the gradient (momentum) and squared gradient (scale) giving per-parameter adaptive steps. L2 penalty inside Adam is rescaled by the adaptive term; AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient update, restoring true regularisation.

Q13How do you prevent/handle exploding gradients?

Gradient-norm clipping, lower LR with warm-up, correct initialisation, normalisation layers, residual connections, careful mixed-precision (bf16).

Q14Why do residual connections help?

They provide an identity path so gradients flow to early layers (∂y/∂x = ∂F/∂x + I) and let layers learn residual corrections, easing optimisation of very deep nets.

Q15Your model’s training loss is NaN — what do you check?

Data (NaN/inf, extreme values), learning rate too high, log(0) or division by zero, fp16 overflow, bad init, exploding gradients. Reproduce on a small batch, enable anomaly detection, log grad norms.

Q16Explain the vanishing-gradient problem in RNNs and the LSTM fix.

Gradients are products of Jacobians over time and shrink exponentially. LSTM adds an additive cell-state path controlled by gates so the derivative along the cell state can stay close to 1.

Q17Describe dropout at train vs inference.

Train: zero each unit with prob p and scale by 1/(1−p). Inference: use all units unchanged (inverted dropout). Acts like averaging many sub-networks.

15.3 Transformers & LLMs

Q18Walk through self-attention and its complexity.

Project X to Q,K,V; scores = QKᵀ/√d; softmax with mask; multiply by V. O(n²d) time, O(n²) memory. FlashAttention removes the n² memory via tiling; sparse/linear attention and SSMs reduce compute.

Q19What is the KV-cache and why does decoding become memory-bound?

Stores keys/values of past tokens so each step only computes attention for the new token. Each decode step reads all weights and the cache but performs few FLOPs — arithmetic intensity is low, so bandwidth limits speed. Mitigate with GQA, quantisation, batching, paged caches.

Q20Explain RoPE.

Rotary embeddings rotate each pair of query/key dimensions by an angle proportional to position; the dot-product then depends only on relative distance. Scaling the frequencies (PI, NTK, YaRN) extends context length.

Q21LoRA — why does low rank suffice?

Fine-tuning updates have low intrinsic dimension: ΔW ≈ BA with r≪d captures most adaptation. It trains <1% of parameters, needs little optimiser memory and can be merged for inference.

Q22RLHF vs DPO?

RLHF fits a reward model then optimises the policy with PPO under a KL constraint — powerful but complex. DPO derives a closed-form classification-style loss on preference pairs relative to a reference model — simpler, stable, but offline and dependent on pair quality.

Q23How do you reduce hallucinations in a production LLM app?

Ground with retrieval, require citations, restrict to provided context, lower temperature, add verification (second pass or tool-based checks), allow abstention, evaluate with a labelled set, and monitor user feedback.

Q24How would you evaluate a RAG system?

Retrieval: recall@k, MRR, nDCG on labelled query→chunk pairs. Generation: faithfulness (claims supported by context), answer relevance, correctness vs gold answers, citation accuracy. Plus latency, cost and human review of failures.

Q25Long-context vs RAG?

Long context is simple but costly (n² attention, KV memory) and suffers ‘lost in the middle’; RAG is cheaper and updatable but adds retrieval error. Use RAG for large/changing corpora, long context for deep reasoning over a few documents — often combine.

Q26What is speculative decoding and is it lossless?

A cheap draft model proposes several tokens; the target model verifies them in parallel and accepts a prefix using a rejection-sampling rule that preserves the target distribution exactly — lossless, gives ≈2–3× speed-up.

15.4 MLOps & system design

Q27How do you detect and respond to model drift?

Monitor input feature distributions (PSI/KS), prediction distribution and delayed-label metrics; alert on thresholds; investigate upstream changes; retrain or roll back via champion/challenger and canary release.

Q28What is training-serving skew and how to prevent it?

Differences between features at training and serving (code paths, time windows, missing values). Prevent with a shared feature store/transform code, logging serving features for training, and integration tests comparing both paths.

Q29Design an online-learning or continuous-training system.

Log predictions + features + outcomes, join delayed labels, validate data, retrain on schedule/trigger, evaluate against champion on fresh slices, gated automatic promotion, staged rollout, monitoring and rollback.

Q30How do you A/B test a ranking model?

Randomise by user, define primary KPI + guardrails, compute sample size from MDE, run full weekly cycles, check SRM (sample-ratio mismatch), use CUPED for variance reduction, beware novelty/network effects.

Q31Cost-optimise an LLM feature.

Route easy queries to small models, cache (semantic + prefix), shorten prompts, batch, quantise/distil, cap output tokens, use RAG instead of long contexts, and monitor $/successful task.

16.4Final 24-hour checklist

  • Re-derive: linear/logistic regression gradient, backprop for a 2-layer MLP, softmax-CE gradient, attention with shapes.
  • Prepare 3 STAR stories and a 2-minute crisp walkthrough of your best project (problem, data, model, metric, impact, what you’d change).
  • Rehearse two system designs aloud (one classic ML, one LLM/RAG) with numbers: QPS, latency, storage, cost.
  • Practise 3 coding problems in Python + 1 SQL window-function query; keep a note of shape checks and edge cases.
  • Sleep well. Clarify assumptions early, think aloud, and structure answers with ABCD.
INTERVIEW TIP Good luck! Depth beats breadth: knowing why each technique works — and where it breaks — is what distinguishes a strong AI/ML engineer.
